chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Hilal, from his father, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

I said to him: Inform me about the thief: why is his right hand and left foot cut, and not his right hand and right foot? He said: “How excellent is what you have asked. If his right hand and right foot were cut, he would fall upon his left side and would not be able to stand. But if his right hand and left foot are cut, he remains balanced and stands upright.”

I said to him: May I be made your ransom, and how does he stand when his foot has been cut? He said: “The cutting is not where you think it is cut. Rather, the foot is cut from the ankle, and enough of his foot is left for him to stand upon, pray, and worship his Lord.”
I said to him: From where is the hand cut? He said: “The four fingers are cut, and the thumb is left, so that he may rely on it in salat (prayer), and with it wash his face for salat (prayer).”
I said: Then this manner of cutting—who was the first to implement it? He said: “'Uthman ibn 'Affan had approved that for Mu'awiyah.”

key_terms.السَّارِقِ: the thief, the person subject to the legal punishment being discussed
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), mentioned as a reason for leaving part of the limb intact
key_terms.الْإِبْهَامُ: the thumb, which is left intact
key_terms.الْكَعْبِ: the ankle, indicating the point from which the foot is cut
key_terms.الْيُسْرَى: the left side, specifically the left foot here
key_terms.الْيُمْنَى: the right side, specifically the right hand here
key_terms.تُقْطَعُ: is cut; refers to the prescribed legal amputation
key_terms.يَعْبُدُ: worships, showing continued ability to worship after the punishment

ai.seo_question: Why is a thief’s right hand and left foot cut in Islamic law instead of the right hand and right foot?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the legal manner of carrying out the punishment for theft, clarifying why the right hand and left foot are cut rather than the right hand and right foot. It also specifies the anatomical limits of the cutting so that the person can still stand, perform salat (prayer), and worship. The report closes with a historical note about the early implementation of this ruling.
